transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-17
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (CTO - Atlanticore), Priya Nair (Eng Lead), Samir Patel (DevOps)
Shared links: https://redwood.ai/pilot-bench (redwood lab notes), https://sheets.redwood.ai/atlc-pilot-bench (raw CSVs)

Summary (auto): quick readout of the last two bench runs; discuss differences vs baseline vendor; agree on head-to-head plan and outstanding security questions.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — results summary, tuning notes, security asks, and next steps. jordan, priya — anything to add before we jump in?
[00:12] Jordan: no, this looks good. keen to see the delta vs our incumbent; last week you said quantize runs were going to land around similar cost but better latency, so let's see the numbers.
[00:25] Diego: great. i'll share screens after the high-level points. note upfront: we ran three traffic shapes — single-shot 128 tokens, 512 tokens, and a bursty 50-concurrency 1k token run. we also toggled KV cache and two batch-size configs.
[00:40] Priya: cool, can you first say which model family you were using — to make sure apples-to-apples? our baseline is using a 13B optimized rp model from OpenCloud AI.
[00:51] Diego: yes — we used Redwood-medium-13b-4q (4-bit) which is our quantized medium variant. weights are slightly different architecture, but we've matched prompt templates and tokenization to your payloads.
[01:05] Samir: small note — for the baseline runs we kept a persistent pool of 8 nodes; curious how you're managing process warmup and k-v cache on your side.
[01:17] Diego: good call. our runs used a warmed runtime with persistent KV cache between related calls for the burst tests; warmup time accounted for in the CSVs.
[01:30] Maya: okay, numbers. diego, do the p50/p95 numbers then the throughput notes.
[01:36] Diego: p50 for 512-token workload: baseline vendor = 410ms, redwood quantized run = 335ms median — so about 18% improvement. p95 baseline = 860ms, redwood = 690ms so about 20% improvement but we noticed a tail spike cluster around 2.2s under sustained concurrency when cache misses occur.
[01:58] Jordan: that tail is concerning — our SLO is 95th under 700ms. you're just inside but spikes worry me. any hypothesis?
[02:09] Diego: hypothesis is twofold: first, cold KV cache or cache eviction under higher concurrency; second, some pathological kernel path at sequence >900 tokens causing memory thrash. we've flagged both and put mitigations in dev backlog: more aggressive per-shard cache pinning and fallback to smaller attention kernel for long sequences.
[02:30] Priya: can you clarify eviction policy? we have a lot of similar user prefixes so caching is critical for us.
[02:36] Diego: current eviction is LRU per GPU with a soft cap tuned during the run. for the next head-to-head we'll try pinning hot prefixes and also measure hit-rate explicitly.
[02:48] Maya: throughput — under sustained 50 concurrency with 1k tokens, baseline sustained ~42 rps, redwood with current batching = ~50 rps. unit-cost looked comparable — Diego, you reported tokens/sec and cost per 1k tokens?
[03:03] Diego: yep. tokens/sec was up ~12% and unit cost per 1k tokens is down around 8% primarily due to quantization and more aggressive batching. caveat: if we force very low latency (batch size 1) cost delta narrows.
[03:20] Jordan: so tradeoff is clear — we can get better throughput and cost with slightly higher latency; we need 95th to be stable.
[03:28] Samir: question on routing/fallback: if a shard fails or runtime OOMs, what's your graceful degradation?
[03:35] Diego: we have policy-based fallback — if a request exceeds latency or memory thresholds, we route to a more conservative model variant (non-quantized medium) or less aggressive batch config. in hosted pilot we can also failover to a dedicated slot we spin up within minutes.
[03:50] Priya: that sounds okay but in enterprise we'll need the failover time guarantees in writing.
[03:55] Maya: noted — i'll put SLA verbiage in the doc i send.
[04:00] Jordan: security — do you support VPC peering for pilot or only IP allowlist? which KMS options?
[04:07] Maya: for pilots we can do IP allowlist; if you need VPC peering we can enable it on Redwood Private path — requires a short setup and an MSA addendum. KMS: we support customer-managed keys via common cloud KMS providers; we can produce the network diagram and SOC2 report.
[04:22] Priya: please send SOC2 plus the network diagram. also, audit log retention policy? we insist on 13 months for this data.
[04:29] Maya: we'll include audit retention options in the packet.
[04:33] Diego: back to perf — one interesting datapoint: when we enable prefix caching for your canonical prompts the p95 drops to ~610ms on 512 tokens, which comfortably meets your SLO. but it's workload dependent. we want to validate with your canonical set.
[04:48] Jordan: can you run a small test using our top-5 prompts?
[04:52] Diego: yes — that's in the next steps.
[04:55] Samir: on infra: for the baseline vendor they used reserved CPUs and kept longer warmup; curious if your warmup patterns are realistic for prod traffic which is spiky.
[05:03] Diego: we can simulate production spikes; in the 30k run we'll include a burst schedule that mirrors your traffic shape.
[05:10] Priya: also want to see error breakdown — timeouts, OOMs, 5xx.
[05:14] Diego: we'll surface that in the CSV and graphs.
[05:18] Maya: pricing — maya: quick question for jordan: what's your threshold for switching vendors? is it purely cost + 95th latency or other factors like operational tooling?
[05:27] Jordan: primarily p95 and predictable cost. but we also evaluate ease of rollback, private deployment options, and observability. we liked the trace-level dashboards from the demo.
[05:36] Maya: good. we're going to include more detailed per-token cost breakdown and route-level traces for the live run.
[05:42] Diego: technical note — for the head-to-head we recommend identical payloads, identical concurrency schedule, and matching cold-start profiles. we'll instrument both sides and capture token-level timing.
[05:54] Priya: if you capture token-by-token timing that helps us identify where attention kernel differences manifest.
[06:00] Diego: agreed. also we'll test with quantized-on vs quantized-off and with different batch sizes: 1, 8, 16.
[06:10] Jordan: any known pitfalls versus our incumbent we should be aware of?
[06:15] Diego: aside from tail due to cache misses, some trading of latency vs cost when you force very low batches; and in our private deployments customers occasionally see slightly higher cold-start for very long sequences — we have a kernel fallback to mitigate.
[06:28] Maya: let's talk scheduling — do we aim for the head-to-head on May 26?
[06:32] Jordan: that works for us tentatively. we'll lock it after we review your updated pricing and SOC2 docs.
[06:38] Samir: one more thing — can you give us a quick sense of quantization regressions on quality? we've seen hallucinations increase a bit in some internal runs.
[06:47] Diego: short answer: on our 5 canonical prompts quality delta was minimal — BLEU/ROUGE-style proxies showed <1.5% delta; but we'll run your exact canonical prompts and include a human spot-check.
[07:00] Priya: okay, good.
[07:05] Maya: wrap-up — recap next steps. diego will run the 30k load and produce CSVs and graphs; maya will send SOC2, network diagram, pricing; customer will confirm VPC need and provide canonical prompts.
[07:18] Jordan: sounds good. appreciate the transparency on tail behavior.
[07:22] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with calendar invites for head-to-head and attach the secure docs.
[07:30] [end of recording]

Notes / artifacts: raw CSVs and graphs exported to https://sheets.redwood.ai/atlc-pilot-bench; replay clip of p95 spike at ~22:14 of the run saved to internal bug tracker.
